Breaking: Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers

📅 26 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that over the past few years, scaling dense language models has driven most progress in LLMs.
  • More data + more parameters gives better performance.
  • Scaling laws reinforced this trend, but dense scaling has practical limits:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that over the past few years, scaling dense language models has driven most progress in LLMs. From early models like the original ULMFiT (~30M parameters) or GPT-2 (1.5B parameters, which at the time was considered "too dangerous to release" 🧌), and eventually to today’s hundred-billion–parameter systems, the recipe was simple:.

More data + more parameters gives better performance.

Scaling laws reinforced this trend, but dense scaling has practical limits:.

This is where Mixture of Experts (MoEs) enter the picture.

If you're already familiar with MoEs and want to jump straight into the engineering work done in transformers, you can head directly to Transformers and MoEs.

Recent findings suggest that A Mixture of Experts model keeps the Transformer backbone, but replaces certain dense feed-forward layers with a set of experts. An “expert” is not a topic-specialized module (e.g., "math expert", "code expert"). It is simply a learnable sub-network. For each token, a router selects a small subset of experts to process it.

Different tokens activate different experts, based on their hidden representations.

Model capacity depends on total parameters, but inference speed depends on active parameters.

For example, take gpt-oss-20b. It has 21B total parameters, but uses 4 active experts per token, out of a total of 32 experts. Considering the shared components plus the active experts, this model uses ~3.6B active parameters per token. Running this model on an M3 Ultra Mac, which has a memory bandwidth of about 800 GB, we could estimate generation speed as ~ 800 / (3.6 * 2) in bfloat16, where each parameter takes 2 bytes. This yields about 111 tokens per second. The actual performance number we get is ~115 tok/s, which is very close to the back-of-the-envelope calculation.

This super fast speed confirms the model works approximately as a 3.6B parameter one, but it has the same capacity (or quality) as a 21B parameter model.

(Note: speed would be even faster if we used kernels for the native mxfp4 quantization the model uses).

MoEs are attractive for these reasons:.

Given a fixed training FLOP budget, MoEs often outperform dense counterparts.

This means faster iteration and better scaling efficiency.

Experts provide a structural boundary in the computation graph. Since different tokens engage different experts, we can parallelize across experts (we discuss this later in Expert Parallelism).

Recent major MoE releases of open models that happened in the past few weeks include Qwen 3.5, MiniMax M2, GLM-5, or Kimi K2.5.

According to recent reports, the trend accelerated after the success of DeepSeek R1 in January 2025, building on earlier systems like DeepSeek V2. Another early MoE was Mixtral-8x7B, released in December 2023.

It has been revealed that closed labs use MoEs too. ChatGPT has long been rumored to use a sparse architecture, and the open gpt-oss models certainly do.

If you want to learn more about MoEs in general, we strongly suggest reading this blog and watching our recent YouTube video on routing.

In a recent development, most tooling in the ecosystem, including model loading, device placement, quantization, and backend execution was originally designed for dense models. MoEs challenge these assumptions.

Making MoEs first-class citizens in transformers means redesigning parts of the loading pipeline, execution model, and distributed abstractions, not just adding new model classes. We’ll focus on how the transformers library has evolved to support sparse architectures across:.

AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("model_id") downloads and loads model weights into a PyTorch model. For dense models, loading is relatively straightforward where each tensor in the checkpoint maps one-to-one to a parameter in the runtime module.

According to recent reports, for MoEs, it’s more complicated. In most MoE checkpoints, each expert is serialized independently. If you peek inside the DeepSeek-V3 checkpoint index, you’ll see keys like:.

In a recent development, each expert has its own set of weight matrices, essentially 256 (0 to 255 total, taking DeepSeek-V3 as an example) small feed-forward networks saved side by side. At runtime, however, GPUs execute optimized kernels. Modern MoE kernels such as grouped GEMMs and fused MoE implementations are designed to process all experts in a single operation, not by looping over them one at a time.

To do that efficiently, they require expert weights to be packed into a single contiguous tensor.

Bridging this gap systematically is what the weight loading refactor enables.

With the introduction of a generic WeightConverter, the mental model shifted from:.

A checkpoint already matches my runtime layout; loading is mostly a key-by-key copy.

A checkpoint is just a serialized source of tensors. Loading is a conversion pipeline that transforms them into the runtime layout we want.

The central abstraction introduced by this refactor is dynamic weight loading via a WeightConverter.

WeightConverter lets us define:.

It has been revealed that primitive operations (chunk, concatenate, etc.) are composable. Two that are particularly useful for MoEs:.

MergeModulelist merges a list of tensors into a single tensor. For example, you can compose MergeModulelist with Concatenate to stack the experts in a MoE and pack them into one tensor.

In a recent development, splitModulelist splits a tensor back into a list of tensors. For example, you can split a stack of experts back into individual experts.

The refactor improves not just what conversions exist, but how they’re scheduled.

It has been revealed that the loader scans checkpoint keys once, matches them against converter patterns, and groups tensors per converter. Once a key is identified as needed, it’s registered as a future and materialized via a thread pool. Conversion operations run only once their dependencies are ready. For example, MergeModulelist waits until all experts for a layer are loaded.

This avoids repeated scans and reduces memory peaks.

To evaluate the improvements introduced by the new weight-loading pipeline, we benchmarked the v4 vs v5 versions of transformers. The focus is on loading speed of large MoE models, which is often a bottleneck in training and inference.

Two relevant environment variables:.

HF_ENABLE_PARALLEL_LOADING: Enables parallel shard loading via threads.

HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD:Disables the upcoming async pipeline (v5 escape hatch).

Model: Qwen/Qwen1.5-110B-Chat GPU: 1× A100 (80GB).

The speedup is not just “more threads.”.

It’s the combination of Single-pass routing, Async materialization, and Conversion-aware scheduling which together avoid unnecessary materialization and memory peaks while enabling expert packing and projection fusion at load time.

Recent findings suggest that with this refactor we can now create the runtime module structure first and then convert the weights into the structure. We can now optionally attach quantization within the conversion pipeline, making quantization part of the weight loading pipeline itself. This is crucial because quantizing “per expert” only makes sense once experts exist in a predictable packed layout.

This end to end pipeline was not possible earlier and now it comes to the users as an exposed API.

Once experts are packed into a single runtime tensor, another question arises:.

How do you actually route through them efficiently?

It has been revealed that in a Mixture of Experts model, each token is routed to different experts. This means the runtime must dispatch tokens to their selected expert weights, execute the projections efficiently, apply the routing weights and then collect and reorder the results.

This is what the Experts Backend system (introduced in PR #42697) addresses. The Experts Backend introduces a pluggable execution architecture that decouples expert computation from the model implementation. Instead of hardcoding one dispatch strategy inside each MoE model, the system allows expert layers to dynamically select a backend at runtime.

This is implemented via a decorator pattern:.

The decorator wraps expert classes and dispatches computation to the selected backend automatically.

Three backends are presently provided:.

It has been revealed that eager which loops over the selected experts and applies projections per expert. This is used for correctness reference and debugging.

batched_mm uses the torch.bmm API. This duplicate selected expert weights per token and performs a single batched GEMM. This backend is very well suited for small batch, GPU-heavy workloads where memory is available.

Industry observers note that grouped_mm uses torch._grouped_mm API. Here we sort tokens by expert ID, group them, and then perform a single grouped GEMM. This backend shines with large batches or memory-constrained setups.

Mixture of Experts (MoE) models can have hundreds of billions of parameters (far more than what fits on a single GPU). Expert parallelism (EP) addresses this by distributing experts across multiple devices. Each device loads only its assigned subset of experts, computes for those experts and then participates in result aggregation. This approach scales models to far larger parameter counts without increasing computation cost because each token activates only a few experts.

Expert parallelism is enabled via enable_expert_parallel:.

Where N evenly divides the total number of experts, and possibly matches the number of GPUs in your node.

When enable_expert_parallel=True, the model switches from the standard tensor-parallel (TP) plan to an expert-parallel (EP) plan with specialized sharding strategies.

Sources indicate that groupedGemmParallel: This splits the expert weights along the expert dimension (dim=0). Here each device loads only num_experts / num_devices.

RouterParallel: This remaps global expert indices to local indices, masks out experts not assigned to the current rank, ensures each device computes only with its local experts and uses an all-reduce to combine partial outputs across devices.

MoEs are excellent for scaling inference, but training them is significantly more complex.

Recent findings suggest that moEs have a Massive parameter count, the distributed expert communication is complicated, there are routing in-stabilities that need to be handled. To address this, we collaborated with Unsloth to enable significantly faster Mixture-of-Experts training:.

We leverage the Expert Backend abstraction, standardize around PyTorch’s torch._grouped_mm API and use custom Triton grouped-GEMM + LoRA kernels. Unsloth builds on top of the Transformers (and TRL) optimizations to push performance further.

For full details, we recommend reading: Unsloth’s official guide.

Recent findings suggest that as sparse architectures continue to evolve, we want the transformers library to evolve with them. If you’re building with MoEs or experimenting with newly introduced sparse ideas, we’d love to hear from you. Let us know what abstractions, kernels, or workflows you’d like to see next in transformers.

The enable_expert_parallel flag hiding the complexity of GroupedGemmParallel + RouterParallel behind a single config is a great DX win — distributing experts across devices used to require a lot of custom plumbing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The smart glasses race is heating up as Meta and Samsung are about to go head-to-head, but could a latest Meta glasses style fix the privacy stigma, or are things too far gone?

Industry observers note that meta launched its own-branded smart glasses this summer (read: with no Ray-Ban or Oakley branding), and they seem to have done well for a number of reasons. Some models are much cheaper than Ray-Ban-branded pairs, while other Meta glasses carry Kylie Jenner or LISA names, bringing in a unique note of fashion, but none of these models changed the look of the camera LED indicator on the front.

According to recent reports, meta has come under fire over the past two years as people have abused the firm’s smart glasses, giving them the unfortunate term “perv glasses” on social media because some people disabled the camera LED, which is supposed to illuminate when the camera is recording. Meta has issued several different software patches to disable the glasses’ camera when the LED is tampered with, but many have begun to feel like having a camera on smart glasses just feels wrong after people have abused the technology.

Meta glasses product lead David Woodland posted a render of the Gentle Monster cateye style glasses in a now-deleted Tweet on X on November 17, simply saying “I plead the fifth.” Presumably, he was calling out how similar these glasses look to the Meta Starfire Kylie Jenner style, but we’ll likely never know now.

Samsung and Google’s Warby Parker and Gentle Monster glasses certainly resemble Meta’s glasses, but they also do something noticeably different: the camera LED doesn’t look like the camera on the other side.

According to recent reports, so this begs the question: can Meta do anything to salvage the unsavory association its glasses now have attached to them? We covered this topic on episode 125 of our Pixelated podcast, and Woodland’s post further highlights the question. A camera LED that’s obviously different from the camera on the other side would likely prompt people to ask about your glasses, while Meta’s design is purposefully stealthy because of its symmetry.

It has been revealed that does this design difference help Samsung’s Gentle Monster/Warby Parker glasses feel more private, and would a similar redesign help Meta’s glasses? I think it would help a lot, but I also want to know what our readers think. What say you, folks?

#80612. Your best people are training your AI. Pay them for it

Your best people are training your AI. Pay them for it

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1751 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, early this year, we let every employee at ClickUp build their own AI agents and skills.
  • According to recent reports, early this year, we let every employee at ClickUp build their own AI agents and skills.
  • When we looked into which AIs brought the most value, there was an obvious pattern.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, early this year, we let every employee at ClickUp build their own AI agents and skills. Within months, we were running five agents for every employee, which felt like a transformation until we looked at the actual output and efficiency. In my own finance org, only 30% of employee-built agents and skills actually moved the needle. When we looked into which AIs brought the most value, there was an obvious pattern. The successful agents were created by employees who understood where a process in their work typically tends to break, and could turn that knowledge into clear rules and processes for artificial intelligence. We went from treating AI skill-building as an open invitation and instead focused on the people who were building AI agents that moved the needle. That fixed the quality problem, but handed us a harder problem to solve. When you take your best talent’s craft and turn it into an AI agent, what does that employee get in return for their expertise and labor? As more companies have the best employees train their AI, leaders must have a response to this question. Define the bar, then pay against it When we changed our AI skill-building process, eligibility depended on a manager’s recommendation and a strong performance review. But identifying the right people is half the work. Companies also need to establish what qualifies as a high-value skill, and what it is worth, before anyone starts building one. We created a framework that categorizes skills, assigns value, and determines the reward. It’s simple but makes it clear what employees should aim for and gives us a consistent way to reward them. At ClickUp, every skill falls into one of four categories, and each category has its own measure of success. One, revenue acceleration skills are measured by the pipeline or bookings they add, and two, cost elimination skills are measured by the spend they remove, like canceling a software we no longer use. Time compression skills, three, are measured by how much faster a core process runs, like closing the books or responding to a customer. And executive bounties, four, are specific problems our leadership team has identified, each with a reward attached. The category tells employees what type of skills to build with AI, but the proof of impact is what determines how much the AI skill is worth. Before creating a latest AI skill, employees must record where the measure stands today, like how many sales meetings aren’t rebooked each month or how long it takes to close the books. Then they can build, and once the AI skill has been running long enough to show a consistent pattern of value, finance compares the new numbers against the starting point. Finance then subtracts the cost of running the AI skill, including tools and maintenance, and what remains is the value the employee created. We then look at what we would have paid to get the same result a different way. Hiring even a few experienced sellers is a major expense, so when one person’s AI skills deliver that same capacity, a standard raise no longer reflects what their work is worth to the business. To determine the reward, we also consider how long the value will last. A skill that solves a single, contained problem earns a bonus. A skill or system the employee will keep running and improving earns a permanent raise, since the tech giant will keep benefiting from that work every year. Together, these steps give us a dollar amount for each AI skill created, which we can use to determine the compensation ranging from a one-time bonus to becoming part of our “unicorn” group. Unicorns are employees whose AI work changes what an entire team can do, and they receive a merit increase of more than 30% along with eligibility for compensation up to $1 million at the top of the band. For example, one growth operations manager identified 17 places where we were regularly losing potential sales and built 11 AI skills to address them. Those skills recovered hundreds of thousands of dollars in pipeline and increased the number of sales prospects by 25%. They also saved every sales rep about 90 minutes in their day, which is equivalent to seven sellers’ worth of capacity. Because the results were large, verified, and directly tied to revenue, this employee joined our “unicorn” group. Reward your talent for making their expertise reusable Your best people are already training your AI. They are handing over the part of themselves that made them hard to replace, and the company can keep using that knowledge long after they have moved on. Hoarding what only one person knows feels like job security, but it is ultimately a ceiling. The people thriving in this model build the skill, hand over their knowledge, and move to the next problem. Each handoff allows them to take on a bigger, more interesting challenge. This is the model companies should build toward as AI moves deeper into knowledge work—rewarding people for making their expertise reusable. That judgment is intellectual property, and paying for it is how you build AI that works while retaining top talent.

#80611. Tech Report: PRX Part 3 — Training a Text-to-Image Model in 24h!

📅 03 Mar 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1698 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: PRX Part 3 — Training a Text-to-Image Model in 24h!

📅 03 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1698 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the last two posts (Part 1 and Part 2), we explored a wide range of architectural and training tricks for diffusion models.
  • In this post, we want to answer a much more practical question:.
  • What happens when we combine all the tricks that worked?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the last two posts (Part 1 and Part 2), we explored a wide range of architectural and training tricks for diffusion models. We tried to evaluate each idea in isolation, measuring throughput, convergence speed, and final image quality, and tried to understand what actually moves the needle.

In this post, we want to answer a much more practical question:.

What happens when we combine all the tricks that worked?

Instead of optimizing one dimension at a time, we’ll stack the most promising ingredients together and see how far we can push performance under a strict compute budget.

To make things concrete, we’re doing a 24-hour speedrun:.

This is very far from the early diffusion days, where training competitive models could cost millions of dollars. The goal here is to demonstrate how much the field has evolved and how far careful engineering can take you in just a single day of training.

Industry observers note that this speedrun is not just a fun experiment. It will likely serve as the foundation for our large-scale training recipe going forward.

Alongside the results, we’re also open-sourcing our code (Github link), which contains:.

So you can reproduce, modify, and extend everything yourself.

Now let’s walk through what went into this 24h run.

In a recent development, we use the x-prediction formulation from Back to Basics: Let Denoising Generative Models Denoise [Li and He, 2025]. As seen in Part 2, this enables training directly in pixel space and eliminates the need for a VAE altogether. We use a patch size of 32 and use a 256-dimensional bottleneck in the initial token projection layer. This design keeps the sequence length under control, making pixel-space training computationally manageable even at higher resolutions.

At 512px, the sequence length is:.

(512/32)2=256 (512 / 32)^2 = 256 (512/32)2=256.

At 1024px, the sequence length becomes:.

(1024/32)2=1024 (1024 / 32)^2 = 1024 (1024/32)2=1024.

Instead of following the usual 256px → 512px → 1024px schedule, we start directly at 512px and then fine-tune at 1024px.

According to recent reports, with controlled token counts and modern hardware, pixel-space training is no longer prohibitive. It is simply a cleaner and more direct formulation.

One very nice side effect of predicting x0x_0x0​ directly in pixel space is that we can reuse a whole toolbox from classical computer vision.

Sources indicate that when your model outputs latents, perceptual supervision becomes awkward. You either have to decode back to pixels or define losses in a learned latent space that may or may not align with human perception. Once you predict pixels directly, everything becomes straightforward again. You can plug in perceptual losses exactly as they were originally designed.

It has been revealed that we take inspiration from the paper PixelGen: Pixel Diffusion Beats Latent Diffusion with Perceptual Loss [Ma et al.], where the authors introduce additional perceptual objectives on top of the diffusion loss. They show that adding perceptual signals can noticeably improve convergence speed and final visual quality.

For this 24h run, we add two auxiliary losses:.

The idea is simple: In addition to the standard flow matching objective, we encourage the predicted clean image to match the target image in a perceptual feature space. LPIPS captures low-level perceptual similarity, while DINO features provide a stronger semantic signal.

We keep the same overall idea as the paper, but we tweaked a few details. In our experiments, we empirically found that it worked better to:.

These are small implementation details, but in our setting they consistently gave better results.

We used a weight of 0.1 for the LPIPS loss and 0.01 for the DINO perceptual loss, matching the values recommended in the original paper.

These losses are lightweight compared to the main transformer forward pass, and in our setup they add only a small overhead while providing a consistent quality boost.

To make each step cheaper, we use token routing with TREAD [Krause et al., 2025]), which randomly selects a fraction of tokens and lets them bypass a contiguous chunk of transformer blocks, then re-injects them later so nothing is dropped.

In a recent development, we picked TREAD over SPRINT (Park et al., 2025) mostly for simplicity, and because the extra complexity of SPRINT did not feel worth the fairly small additional compute savings in our setting (sequence length 64 vs. 128 with TREAD at 512px).

Following the TREAD recipe, we route 50% of the tokens from the 2nd block to the penultimate block of the transformer.

Routed models can look worse under vanilla CFG, especially when undertrained, so we implemented a simple self-guidance scheme inspired by Guiding Token-Sparse Diffusion Models (Krause et al., 2025), which guides using a dense vs. routed conditional prediction instead of relying on an unconditional branch.

We used REPA [Yu et al., 2024] for representation alignment.

Recent findings suggest that for the teacher, we went with DINOv3 [Siméoni et al. 2025] since it gave the best quality improvements in our previous experiments.

Concretely, we apply the alignment loss once,at the 8th transformer block with a loss weight of 0.5.

According to recent reports, since we combine REPA with TREAD routing, we only compute the alignment loss on the non-routed tokens, meaning the tokens that actually go through the blocks where we apply the loss. This keeps the REPA signal consistent and avoids comparing features for tokens that skipped the computation path.

We used the Muon optimizer, using the FSDP implementation from muon_fsdp_2, since it showed a clear improvement over Adam in our previous runs.

Muon is only applied to 2D parameters (basically matrices). Everything else (biases, norms, embeddings, etc.) is optimized with Adam, which is why the config has two parameter groups.

We trained on three publicly available synthetic datasets:.

The schedule is basically: go fast at 512, then sharpen at 1024:.

We also keep an EMA of the weights for sampling and eval:.

Below are the evaluation curves we tracked throughout the run and a few sample grids from the final checkpoint:.

For a one day training run, this is already a pretty solid place to be. The model is not flawless yet (you can still spot some texture glitches, occasional weird anatomy, and it can get a bit shaky on very hard prompts), but it is clearly usable. Prompt following is strong, the overall aesthetic is consistent, and the 1024 stage mostly does what we want: sharpen details without breaking composition.

According to recent reports, the key takeaway is that we're very close. The remaining complications look more like undertraining artifacts and limited data diversity than signs of a structural flaw in the recipe. The failure modes are consistent with what you’d expect from a model that simply hasn’t seen enough varied data yet. With more compute and broader coverage, this exact setup should continue improving in a fairly predictable way.

Sources indicate that zooming out, this speed run also highlights how far diffusion training has come. By combining pixel-space training, efficient routing, representation alignment, and lightweight perceptual guidance, you can now get a meaningful model in about a day on a budget that would have sounded unrealistic not that long ago.

This 24h run is just a starting point, not the finish line. Next, we will keep pushing the same recipe with a bit more scale and iterate on the dataset mix and captioning.

All the code and configs behind this speedrun, as well as the full experimental framework used throughout Part 1 and Part 2, are available in the PRX repository: https://github.com/Photoroom/PRX.

While we don’t redistribute the exact training datasets used in this run, the pipeline is fully configurable and designed to be easily adapted to your own data. You can plug in different datasets, tweak individual components (TREAD, REPA, perceptual losses, Muon, etc.), and run controlled experiments with minimal friction. Our goal is to make this a practical playground for fast diffusion research, and we hope the community will use it to explore, benchmark, and iterate on these techniques in their own setups.

Sources indicate that if you made it this far, thank you for reading. We would also love to have you join our Discord community, where we share PRX progress and results, and discuss anything diffusion and text-to-image related.

It has been revealed that goodbye for now, and stay tuned for the next round of experiments! 🚀.

In a recent development, this speedrun was inspired by several recent efforts exploring fast and low-cost training of diffusion models. If you're interested in speedrunning text-to-image models, we encourage you to check out the following works:.

Yeah, definitely not possible on consumer hardware… yet :D That’s also why we added the $1500 tag.

In a recent development, regarding releasing the captions, we hadn’t really thought about that. If you think it would be valuable for the community, we can work on releasing them as well.

Hi, this article is very inspiring.I'd like to get your thoughts on the perceptual loss. During a research internship on (raw) image restoration - and trying to explore the perception/distortion tradeoff , I did a few attempts at VGG and Dino loss aswell. I always ended up with checkerboard patterns (no matter vgg or dino). If you look at the original paper from Johnson , it's full of these artifacts.Did you face any such issue or can share useful insights about that topic ?

It has been revealed that I don’t think we really observed such artifacts, or at least not due to LPIPS. We did see something similar without LPIPS when using JIT on undertrained models, but I don’t think we observe them anymore. It might simply be because the model had not converged yet.One situation where we started to observe checkerboard patterns was during reward alignment with GRPO or SRPO on one of these models. There’s zero reason to store your SS card like this. Unnecessary exposure.

According to recent reports, while exact functionality is unclear at this time, this appears to include support for seeing your Social Security benefits, or at least logging those benefits, in a digital form. The weakest link in cybersecurity is still a human one

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1953 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the end of Jensen Huang’s tenure at Nvidia is steeped in irony.
  • In a recent development, the end of Jensen Huang’s tenure at Nvidia is steeped in irony.
  • Industry observers note that huang’s resignation from the chipmaker he cofounded followed reports of multiple affairs, most notably one with Alice Huang, a business executive U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the end of Jensen Huang’s tenure at Nvidia is steeped in irony. The chief executive of a organization whose growth has been propelled by the seemingly unstoppable rise of artificial intelligence was brought down by a vulnerability that no algorithm can eliminate: human nature. Huang’s resignation from the chipmaker he cofounded followed reports of multiple affairs, most notably one with Alice Huang, a business executive U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China. The company states no secrets were leaked. In a world increasingly focused on protecting private information against high-tech hacking schemes, Huang’s downfall is a reminder that, as the infamous hacker Kevin Mitnick observed, the “human factor is truly security’s weakest link.” Huang is hardly the first person in a powerful position to lower their defenses. In 2023, Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni spoke candidly about foreign affairs in a call with Russian pranksters who recorded and released the conversation. In 2011, former CIA Director David Petraeus gave his biographer, with whom he was having an affair, access to notebooks containing classified information. These cases raise an important question: Why would someone with an entire security apparatus at their disposal let their guard down in an ordinary conversation or an intimate moment? Part of the answer comes down to the ways in which we are wired to react to other human beings. As a social psychologist who studies how people respond to requests, I’ve seen how a human voice, a simple touch, or the mere physical presence of another person can be persuasive. Social cues that increase a sense of familiarity and intimacy can make people feel safer, more trusting—and more willing to hand over money, comply with requests, divulge information, or take risks. The comfort of a human voice Mitnick has been called “the most notorious hacker of all time.” Until his arrest in 1995, he spent years gaining access to privileged information at companies such as Nokia and Motorola. He pulled off his espionage not by writing sophisticated code-breaking software but by having conversations with his targets. He would call people up and talk them into handing over their passwords by claiming to be the fresh IT guy or someone’s boss’s colleague. The people he spoke to overwhelmingly believed him. In other words, Mitnick recognized the power of the human voice. Studies show that hearing a person’s voice, as compared to reading their written thoughts, makes that person seem more capable and relatable. Interactions via phone, video chat, and voice chat also create stronger social bonds than the same kinds of interactions via text or email. Perhaps for these reasons, people are more effective at persuading others to do things for them over the phone compared to when they make the same requests by text. In a study I conducted with social psychologist Mahdi Roghanizad, participants asked other people for favors through randomly assigned communication channels. They received about twice as many yes responses over the phone as they did by email. When it comes to obtaining company secrets or circumventing export laws, a human voice may be all you need. And that isn’t the only edge people have. The Midas touch Studies have found that human touch can also have surprising effects on tipping behavior, acquiescence, and risk-taking. In a famous 1984 study, a server who lightly touched diners as she handed them their change received bigger tips. In another classic psychology study, female experimenters approached 178 strangers and asked them for change to use a nearby pay phone. When the experimenters lightly touched the arm of a person they approached, that person was 76% more likely to agree to give the change. In a 2010 study, participants were more willing to take financial risks when a female experimenter gave them a light, comforting pat on their shoulder. The power of face-to-face Perhaps the most well-known study of influence, Stanley Milgram’s infamous shock experiment, illustrates how much it can matter to be in the room when you ask someone to do something they may be feeling uneasy about. In the original study, an experimenter stood behind participants and instructed them to administer purportedly dangerous shocks to someone they thought was just another participant. The experimenter asked participants to incrementally increase the intensity of the shocks. Nearly two-thirds of participants went all the way to the highest shock setting. In a variation of the study, however, the experimenter left the room and gave instructions over the phone. In this version, only 22.5% went that far. Although researchers continue to debate how to interpret Milgram’s findings, my colleagues and I have similarly found that people are far more likely to say yes when we ask them to do something face-to-face. In a recent development, the end of Jensen Huang’s tenure at Nvidia is steeped in irony. The chief executive of a company whose growth has been propelled by the seemingly unstoppable rise of artificial intelligence was brought down by a vulnerability that no algorithm can eliminate: human nature.

Industry observers note that huang’s resignation from the chipmaker he cofounded followed reports of multiple affairs, most notably one with Alice Huang, a business executive U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China. The tech giant states no secrets were leaked.

In a world increasingly focused on protecting private information against high-tech hacking schemes, Huang’s downfall is a reminder that, as the infamous hacker Kevin Mitnick observed, the “human factor is truly security’s weakest link.”.

Huang is hardly the first person in a powerful position to lower their defenses. In 2023, Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni spoke candidly about foreign affairs in a call with Russian pranksters who recorded and released the conversation. In 2011, former CIA Director David Petraeus gave his biographer, with whom he was having an affair, access to notebooks containing classified information.

These cases raise an vital question: Why would someone with an entire security apparatus at their disposal let their guard down in an ordinary conversation or an intimate moment?

Recent findings suggest that part of the answer comes down to the ways in which we are wired to react to other human beings. As a social psychologist who studies how people respond to requests, I’ve seen how a human voice, a simple touch, or the mere physical presence of another person can be persuasive. Social cues that increase a sense of familiarity and intimacy can make people feel safer, more trusting—and more willing to hand over money, comply with requests, divulge information, or take risks.

It has been revealed that mitnick has been called “the most notorious hacker of all time.” Until his arrest in 1995, he spent years gaining access to privileged information at companies such as Nokia and Motorola. He pulled off his espionage not by writing sophisticated code-breaking software but by having conversations with his targets.

Recent findings suggest that he would call people up and talk them into handing over their passwords by claiming to be the new IT guy or someone’s boss’s colleague. The people he spoke to overwhelmingly believed him.

In other words, Mitnick recognized the power of the human voice.

Studies show that hearing a person’s voice, as compared to reading their written thoughts, makes that person seem more capable and relatable. Interactions via phone, video chat, and voice chat also create stronger social bonds than the same kinds of interactions via text or email.

In a recent development, perhaps for these reasons, people are more effective at persuading others to do things for them over the phone compared to when they make the same requests by text. In a study I conducted with social psychologist Mahdi Roghanizad, participants asked other people for favors through randomly assigned communication channels. They received about twice as many yes responses over the phone as they did by email.

When it comes to obtaining firm secrets or circumventing export laws, a human voice may be all you need. And that isn’t the only edge people have.

Studies have found that human touch can also have surprising effects on tipping behavior, acquiescence, and risk-taking.

In a recent development, in a famous 1984 study, a server who lightly touched diners as she handed them their change received bigger tips. In another classic psychology study, female experimenters approached 178 strangers and asked them for change to use a nearby pay phone. When the experimenters lightly touched the arm of a person they approached, that person was 76% more likely to agree to give the change.

In a recent development, the researchers theorized that these light touches created a sense of familiarity. That familiarity, in turn, made people more willing to open their wallets.

It has been revealed that other research suggests that light touch can also make people feel safer and more willing to take risks. In a 2010 study, participants were more willing to take financial risks when a female experimenter gave them a light, comforting pat on their shoulder.

Perhaps the most well-known study of influence, Stanley Milgram’s infamous shock experiment, illustrates how much it can matter to be in the room when you ask someone to do something they may be feeling uneasy about.

According to recent reports, in the original study, an experimenter stood behind participants and instructed them to administer purportedly dangerous shocks to someone they thought was just another participant. The experimenter asked participants to incrementally increase the intensity of the shocks. Nearly two-thirds of participants went all the way to the highest shock setting. In a variation of the study, however, the experimenter left the room and gave instructions over the phone. In this version, only 22.5% went that far.

Although researchers continue to debate how to interpret Milgram’s findings, my colleagues and I have similarly found that people are far more likely to say yes when we ask them to do something face-to-face.

It has been revealed that in one study, participants who made requests in person were 34 times more likely to get a yes than those who made requests by email. In another study, in-person requests were significantly more effective than requests made over the phone or video call.

Cyberattacks and phishing emails pose real threats to security. But sometimes the biggest threats come from the people in the room with you. While we don’t know exactly what transpired between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, her proximity to the Nvidia CEO illustrates a vulnerability that even the best cybersecurity measures can struggle to guard against.

Vanessa Bohns is a Braunstein Family Professor and chair of organizational behavior at Cornell University.

The owner of a dwindling empire of Wendy’s restaurants on Friday disclosed its plans to close several more stores, bringing its total number of shuttered locations to almost 100. It’s a grim milestone for the popular burger chain as it works to execute on a turnaround proposal aimed at boosting sales and bolstering its brand image. The franchisee behind the closures, Meritage Hospitality Group of Grand Rapids, Michigan, is among the largest operators within the Wendy’s system, at one time owning roughly 375 locations across 15 states. It closed dozens of those restaurants in the months before a Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing in September, and has since shuttered additional waves of stores at regular intervals as part of cash collateral agreements with its lenders. How many Wendy’s stores has Meritage closed? According to court documents, Meritage has closed well over 90 Wendy’s locations since late last year, with many of those stores shuttered before its September bankruptcy petition. As is typical in Chapter 11 cases, Meritage is seeking to reject the leases on many of the stores that it closed pre-bankruptcy—roughly 60, court filings show—a list that includes a handful of Taco John’s and Morning Belle locations, in addition to Wendy’s. Since the bankruptcy, Meritage has also closed at least 41 additional Wendy’s restaurants, including six closures that were disclosed on Friday. The newly shuttered restaurants were located in Florida, Georgia, Michigan, and Ohio: 12135 Lem Turner Road Jacksonville, FL 32218 1928 Hwy 155 McDonough, GA 30252 3675 Cascade Road Atlanta, GA 30331 9556 US 31 So Interlochen, MI 49643 8258 Broadmoor Avenue Caledonia, MI 49316 914 Conant St. Maumee, OH 43537 Prior to the above six restaurants, Meritage disclosed waves of store closures on at least five separate occasions: 5 locations on September 25 5 locations on October 2 10 locations on October 9 13 stores on October 16 2 stores on October 30 Fast Company has reached out to Meritage Hospitality Group and Wendy’s for comment. What will happen to Meritage’s remaining stores? Meritage has owned Wendy’s restaurants since the late 1990s, but its relationship with the fast food giant appeared to turn increasingly contentious in recent years as its business faced headwinds on numerous fronts, including the soaring cost of beef. The franchisee has blamed Wendy’s for a strategy of “deep discounting” that it states squeezed profits. The Wendy’s Company, for its part, had sought to terminate Meritage’s franchise agreements, claiming to be owed more than $146 million in past-due royalties and other fees. Despite all this animosity, the two sides are working together to salvage what’s left of the Meritage fleet. Wendy’s disclosed earlier this month that it wants to buy up to 163 restaurants from Meritage. That deal, which is still subject to better bids, is expected to close early next year. Additionally, Meritage is moving to sell restaurants to various other buyers in separate deals, including one to sell 42 locations in Arkansas, Mississippi, Missouri, and Tennessee to an entity called Divine Infinity Operations. It’s unclear if additional Wendy’s locations could close before or after these asset sales are complete. This story is developing….

The franchisee behind the closures, Meritage Hospitality Group of Grand Rapids, Michigan, is among the largest operators within the Wendy’s system, at one time owning roughly 375 locations across 15 states.

It closed dozens of those restaurants in the months before a Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing in September, and has since shuttered additional waves of stores at regular intervals as part of cash collateral agreements with its lenders.

According to court documents, Meritage has closed well over 90 Wendy’s locations since late last year, with many of those stores shuttered before its September bankruptcy petition.

As is typical in Chapter 11 cases, Meritage is seeking to reject the leases on many of the stores that it closed pre-bankruptcy—roughly 60, court filings show—a list that includes a handful of Taco John’s and Morning Belle locations, in addition to Wendy’s.

It has been revealed that since the bankruptcy, Meritage has also closed at least 41 additional Wendy’s restaurants, including six closures that were disclosed on Friday. The newly shuttered restaurants were located in Florida, Georgia, Michigan, and Ohio:.

Meritage has owned Wendy’s restaurants since the late 1990s, but its relationship with the fast food giant appeared to turn increasingly contentious in recent years as its business faced headwinds on numerous fronts, including the soaring cost of beef. The franchisee has blamed Wendy’s for a strategy of “deep discounting” that it says squeezed profits.

The Wendy’s Company, for its part, had sought to terminate Meritage’s franchise agreements, claiming to be owed more than $146 million in past-due royalties and other fees.

Despite all this animosity, the two sides are working together to salvage what’s left of the Meritage fleet. Wendy’s disclosed earlier this month that it wants to buy up to 163 restaurants from Meritage. That deal, which is still subject to better bids, is expected to close early next year.

Additionally, Meritage is moving to sell restaurants to various other buyers in separate deals, including one to sell 42 locations in Arkansas, Mississippi, Missouri, and Tennessee to an entity called Divine Infinity Operations.

It’s unclear if additional Wendy’s locations could close before or after these asset sales are complete.

The pages of a site form a graph. Think of it as many nodes connected to each other via edges. Each of the edges are the links between the pages, and the nodes themselves are the pages. Now if you start to visualize this as a graph, you will quickly see that there are multiple ways to traverse this graph and reach a particular endpoint.

A search crawler usually uses one of these pages as a starting point and crawls through all of the pages (especially when pages are not fully covered in a sitemap).

Industry observers note that if a page lies very deep from the home page, it means that it's not an key page. It's an indication to the search engine that this is not something that you yourself consider important, and the search engine has a lesser incentive to rank this page over pages that are linked better within your site.

The key metric here is link depth. That is the number of clicks it takes to reach a particular page from your home page.

Sources indicate that another key metric is broken links. If you have too many broken links, it indicates to the search engine that your site is outdated and not well maintained, and the search engine will then not want to rank your site.

The way to identify both these problems is the same: to actually walk through your site, do a crawl of your site outside in, and try to figure out what the link depth is and if there are broken links on your website.

It has been revealed that seed the crawl with the home page and all URLs mentioned in the sitemap. Technically, the sitemap is not required if you're doing a crawl, but going from the sitemap will allow us to detect orphaned pages as well.

It has been revealed that fetch the pages and follow redirects as required. Record when you're following a redirect: we do not let fetch follow it silently, we record each hop and add its target to the crawl. Record HTTP errors as they occur.

Drop URL fragments and tracking parameters. Keep trailing slashes because sometimes there can be mismatches around expectation of trailing slashes in different URLs of a site.

In order to navigate from the home page, we can use BFS. So we know that the first time we reach a page, that is the page's shortest path.

We can cut off the depth over a certain threshold, say 5, to indicate that pages beyond that are too far or too deep to be reached.

Noindex pages will still be crawled. However, we need to make a record of them being not indexed, to reflect that they will not be present in the search engine.

The desired page depth is as close to the home page as possible. Notable pages should be close to the home page. The deeper you go from the home page, it signals to the search engine that the page is less important.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Modular Diffusers introduces a latest way to build diffusion pipelines by composing reusable blocks. Instead of writing entire pipelines from scratch, you can mix and match blocks to create workflows tailored to your needs! This complements the existing DiffusionPipeline class with a more flexible, composable alternative.

In this post, we'll walk through how Modular Diffusers works — from the familiar API to run a modular pipeline, to building fully custom blocks and composing them into your own workflow. We'll also show how it integrates with Mellon, a node-based visual workflow interface that you can use to wire Modular Diffusers blocks together.

Here is a simple example of how to run inference with FLUX.2 Klein 4B using pre-built blocks:.

You get the same results as with a standard DiffusionPipeline, but the pipeline is very different under the hood: it's composed of flexible blocks — text encoding, image encoding, denoising, and decoding — that you can inspect directly:.

Each block is self-contained with its own inputs and outputs. You can run any block independently as its own pipeline, or add, remove, and swap blocks freely — they dynamically recompose to work with whatever blocks remain. Use .init_pipeline() to convert blocks into a runnable pipeline, and .load_components() to load the model weights.

For more on block types, composition patterns, lazy loading, and memory management with ComponentsManager, check out the Modular Diffusers documentation.

According to recent reports, modular Diffusers really shines when creating your own blocks. A custom block is a Python class that defines its components, inputs, outputs, and computation logic — and once defined, you can plug it into any workflow.

Here's an example block that extracts depth maps from images using Depth Anything V2.

Let's use this block with Qwen's ControlNet workflow. Extract the ControlNet workflow and insert the depth block at the beginning:.

Blocks in a sequence share data automatically: the depth block's control_image output flows to downstream blocks that need it, and its image input becomes a pipeline input since no earlier block provides it.

It has been revealed that you can publish your custom block to the Hub so anyone can load it with trust_remote_code=True. We've created a template to get you started — check out the Building Custom Blocks guide for the full walkthrough.

The DepthProcessorBlock from this post is published at diffusers/depth-processor-custom-block — you can load and use it directly:.

We've published a collection of ready-to-use custom blocks here.

ModularPipeline.from_pretrained works with any existing Diffusers repo out of the box, but Modular Diffusers also introduces a latest kind of repo: the Modular Repository.

Recent findings suggest that A modular repository is able to reference components from their original model repos. For example, diffusers/flux2-bnb-4bit-modular contains a quantized transformer and loads the remaining components from the original repo.

Modular repositories can also host custom pipeline blocks as Python code and visual UI configurations for tools like Mellon — all in one place.

The community has already started building complete pipelines with Modular Diffusers and publishing them on the Hub, with model weights and ready-to-run code.

Teams can build novel architectures, package them as blocks, and publish the entire pipeline on the Hub for anyone to use with ModularPipeline.from_pretrained.

Check out the full collection of community pipelines for more.

💡 Mellon is in early development and not ready for production use yet. Consider this a sneak peek of how the integration works!

Industry observers note that mellon is a node graph interface integrated with Modular Diffusers. If you're familiar with node-based tools like ComfyUI, you'll feel right at home — but there are some key differences:.

This integration is possible because every block exposes the same properties (inputs, intermediate_outputs, expected_components). This consistent API means Mellon can automatically generate a node's UI from any block definition and compose blocks into higher-level nodes.

Industry observers note that for example, diffusers/FLUX.2-klein-4B-modular contains a pipeline definition, component references, and a mellon_pipeline_config.json — all in one repo. Load it in Python with ModularPipeline.from_pretrained("diffusers/FLUX.2-klein-4B-modular") or in Mellon to create either a single-node or multi-node workflow.

It has been revealed that here's a quick example. We add a Gemini prompt expansion node — hosted as a modular repo at diffusers/gemini-prompt-expander-mellon — to an existing text-to-image workflow:.

In a recent development, gemini expands your short prompt into a detailed description before generating the image. No code, no configuration — just a Hub repo id.

It has been revealed that this is just one example. For a detailed walkthrough, check out the Mellon x Modular Diffusers guide. You can also check out this video!

According to recent reports, modular Diffusers brings the composability and flexibility the community has been asking for, without compromising the features that make Diffusers powerful. It's still early — we want your input to shape what comes next. Give it a try and tell us what works, what doesn't, and what's missing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You unplug your laptop with a full charge, sit down at a coffee shop to get some work done, and an hour later your battery is already at 50%. You check your system settings to see what’s killing your power, and the culprit is exactly what you suspected: your web browser. Modern websites are effectively heavy software applications running constantly in the background. If you keep dozens of tabs open, your browser is caching media, running ad scripts, and refreshing data for every single one of them simultaneously. It eats up your system memory and forces your processor to work overtime. You don’t have to change the way you work or close your research tabs to get your battery life back. You just need to flip a few switches hidden in your browser’s settings menu. Turn on native memory savers Both Chrome and Edge finally have built-in tools to stop background tabs from draining power. In Chrome, go to Settings, click Performance and turn on Memory Saver and choose the Maximum option. In Edge, go to Settings, click System and Performance > Performance, and turn on Enable Energy Saver, then set it to Maximum Savings. Then toggle Automatically Put Tabs to Sleep on. This setting automatically puts inactive tabs to sleep until you click back to them. Stop background apps from running when closed By default, browsers like to keep their background processes running even after you’ve closed the browser window entirely. This is terrible for your battery. Go to Chrome’s Settings, click System, and toggle off the switch that claims “Continue running background apps when Google Chrome is closed.” In Edge, go to System and Performance > System and toggle off “Continue running background extensions and apps when Edge is closed.” Use a tab discarding extension If you’re someone who keeps fifty tabs open at all times, native memory savers might not be aggressive enough. Install a free extension such as Auto Tab Discard. It lets you set strict rules, like automatically unloading any tab you haven’t looked at in 10 minutes. The tab stays visible in your top bar, but it uses absolutely zero battery power until you click it again.

Sources indicate that you unplug your laptop with a full charge, sit down at a coffee shop to get some work done, and an hour later your battery is already at 50%. You check your system settings to see what’s killing your power, and the culprit is exactly what you suspected: your web browser.

It has been revealed that modern websites are effectively heavy software applications running constantly in the background. If you keep dozens of tabs open, your browser is caching media, running ad scripts, and refreshing data for every single one of them simultaneously. It eats up your system memory and forces your processor to work overtime.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent advances in Large Language Models have enabled the transition from text-only reasoning to multimodal systems.
  • In synchronous control pipelines, while the VLA is running inference, the arm is idle awaiting commands leading to oscillatory behavior and delayed corrections.
  • Sources indicate that bringing VLA models to embedded platforms is not a matter of model compression, but a complex systems engineering problem requiring architectural decomposition, latency-aware scheduling, and hardware-aligned execution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Authors: Enzo Ruedas, Tess Boivin.

Recent advances in Large Language Models have enabled the transition from text-only reasoning to multimodal systems. First, with the integration of visual perception in Vision–Language Models (VLMs), and more recently with the generation of robot actions in Vision–Language–Action (VLA) models. Deploying these models on embedded robotic platforms remains a challenge due to tight constraints in terms of compute, memory, and power, as well as real-time control requirements.

In synchronous control pipelines, while the VLA is running inference, the arm is idle awaiting commands leading to oscillatory behavior and delayed corrections. To tackle that, asynchronous Inference can enable smooth and continuous motion by dissociating generation from execution. However, to be effective, the end-to-end inference latency must remain shorter than the action execution duration. This temporal constraint therefore sets an upper limit on the model's throughput.

Sources indicate that bringing VLA models to embedded platforms is not a matter of model compression, but a complex systems engineering problem requiring architectural decomposition, latency-aware scheduling, and hardware-aligned execution. Addressing these challenges is essential to translate recent advances in multimodal foundation models into practical and deployable embedded robotic systems.

This guide presents NXP’s hands‑on best practices for recording reliable robotic datasets, fine‑tuning VLA policies (ACT and SmolVLA), and hightlights the real-time performance that NXP i.MX 95 SoC achieves after optimization.

High‑quality, consistent data beats “more but messy” data. This section turns hard‑earned lessons into concrete checklists and schemas.

In our case, we recorded a dataset for the task: "Put the tea bag in the mug.".

Sources indicate that moving from scene‑only views to mixed viewpoints increases the global accuracy, but the more cameras you have the more the latency is impacted. Therefore, you must choose right compromise. In our case that balance was reached with 3 cameras:.

We strongly recommend using a gripper-mounted camera. It consistently improves success rates on fine manipulation tasks by providing a close, task-relevant viewpoint. Importantly, it is also the camera that most effectively enforces correct data collection practices, allowing the operator to rely exclusively on the robot’s perception rather than observing the scene directly.

When installing a gripper camera, we recommend securing the cable with Velcro or a strain-relief guide to prevent it from obstructing the field of view or becoming disconnected during motion.

Simple hardware tweaks like heat‑shrink tubing over gripper claws increase friction, reduce roughness, reduce slippage during episodes, and increase task success rate (fewer “almost success” episodes), improving policy learning stability.

When recording a dataset, you should:.

Vary episodes distribution: Divide your workspace into starting-position clusters, and record at least 10 episodes per cluster. Add diversity by changing the object position and rotation.

e.g. we partitioned the robot arm’s reachable workspace into 11 clusters, each measuring 10 × 10 cm.

Differentiate training & validation sets: Policies can easily overfit on the training set, so make sure that the validation set is unseen by the model.

e.g. we removed cluster 6 from the training set.

Record the most movements you can: Small VLA models exhibit limited generalization on unseen motion. Therefore, record episodes that cover the wider ranges of degrees of freedom.

e.g. we grasped the tea bag either in horizontal or vertical position.

Recent findings suggest that anticipate failure: Sometimes the policy will not reach the object the first time and will have to "go back to it". We noticed that having 20% of all episodes that corresponds to the case of going back to the object help the model improve overall success rate.

Industry observers note that e.g. around 20% of our training set corresponds to recovery episodes.

This mirrors best practices across VLA papers and community guides. Here are 3 examples of data diversity within the same cluster:.

Sources indicate that starting positions 1 and 2 correspond to different positions within the same cluster. In contrast, during the recovery episode, the robot does not begin in "starting mode"; but is instead already near the mug and should proceed directly to retrieve the tea bag from that location.

The range providing the best trade-off between accuracy, generalization, and motion smoothness across both the training and validation sets was found for ACT (100 actions per chunk) within a 100k-160k training steps. For SMolVLA training (50 actions per chunk), the trade‑off appears after many more training steps. We found that continuing training slightly past the point where the model begins to overfit tends to improve overall accuracy.

Rule of thumb: choose final checkpoint by evaluating success on both training and validation set, not by training loss.

The i.MX 95 SoC integrates 6× Arm Cortex‑A55, a Cortex‑M7 and a Cortex M33 MCU, a Mali GPU, a fresh NXP ISP, and the eIQ® Neutron NPU, targeting efficient, secure edge inference with multi‑camera support and strong I/O. [nxp.com].

Industry observers note that instead of running the models as one monolithic graph, we decompose the VLA graph into logical stages: encoders, decoders, and action experts. Therefore, allowing each component to be optimized, scheduled, and deployed independently.

In practice, SmolVLA is partitioned into the following sub-blocks:.

It has been revealed that this separation allows per-block optimizations. The impact of each block quantization can be measured to choose the best tradeoff between latency and accuracy. Also, isolating the action expert from the VLM was ideal to run it at lower frequency.

It has been revealed that in order to optimize the inference for i.MX 95 SoC, we explored several quantization techniques on different blocks. We found that quantizing the vision encoder and LLM prefill had limited impact on accuracy, whereas quantization of the denoising flow in the action expert significantly degrades performance.This behaviour is expected, as quantization errors are accumulating across iterative denoising steps.

That is why we decided to keep this block at higher precision to preserve stability, while on the other blocks, we explored various quantization configurations, from 8-bit mixed precision to 4-bit quantization, depending on the layers.

According to recent reports, in addition, we applied in-house optimization on the different blocks. Results are shown in the below table, referred as optimized models.

With Asynchronous Inference, action generation runs in parallel with execution:.

This increases effective control frequency, reduces observation staleness, and improves recovery behavior.

On embedded platforms such as the i.MX 95 SoC, asynchronous inference is essential — but only effective if inference latency is kept under the action horizon budget: inference time < execution time.

Our immediate objective is to improve task accuracy with SmolVLA (ONNX FP32). We have already established a baseline and measured an optimized on-board inference latency of 6.15 s.

It has been revealed that the next phase will focus on deeper optimizations on our NPUs. In parallel, we aim to move from single-task setup toward longer-horizon and more complex scenarios. To do that, we will introduce:.

Tech Report: Fitbit Edge after 30 days: Life in the middle lane [Video]

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1473 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The biggest compliment you can pay Google at the moment is that alongside the Pixel Watch, recent Fitbit releases have been a huge return to form – the Fitbit Edge included.
  • I need to nail my colors to the mast; I’m a Fitbit Air fanboy.
  • Industry observers note that the Fitbit Edge worried me at first because it comes with a screen, which is something I realized isn’t that notable to me day-to-day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The biggest compliment you can pay Google at the moment is that alongside the Pixel Watch, recent Fitbit releases have been a huge return to form – the Fitbit Edge included.

I need to nail my colors to the mast; I’m a Fitbit Air fanboy. I’ve talked about it multiple times on the Pixelated podcast, here on the site, and it made me switch away from the Pixel Watch 5 because of how easily it fit into my existence without insisting on itself.

Industry observers note that the Fitbit Edge worried me at first because it comes with a screen, which is something I realized isn’t that notable to me day-to-day. After 30 days of wear, I’m conflicted because maybe I was too hasty to ditch a display on my wrist.

It has been revealed that the design is somewhat in a halfway house because it feels like it’s trying to be both a classic Fitbit while integrating some of the Pixel Watch features we know and love. Initially, I loved it, but it has become something that isn’t quite enough in either direction to suit my own tastes.

My love for the simplicity of the Fitbit Air has colored how I feel, but the Edge has an excellent core design. The display bezels remind me heavily of the original Pixel Watch; yes, they’re there, but you only notice them when the light catches the frame edge.

After a month of daily wear, the display has lost a bit of its luster. The oleophobic coating is just about holding up, but now we’re into the cooler months; it’ll be put through a barrage of jacket cuffs and hoodie sleeves. This is one of the only durability concerns I have had so far.

Industry observers note that despite that admittedly minor concern, the Fitbit Edge is not something you need to baby. I’ve bashed it with weights, caught my wrist on zips (zippers for you, my American friends), and bashed it around with reckless abandon. It’s solid and hasn’t picked up as much as a single scuff. I don’t care too much if a fitness tracker gets a beating, whereas I would be more concerned about damaging my Pixel Watch.

If you come in wanting a smartwatch-like experience from the Fitbit Edge, I think you’ll instantly be frustrated by the UI. It can feel cramped when you see notifications, and the large bezels don’t help all that much, but Google has well optimized almost all of the key sections outside of this.

In a recent development, tiles are very well implemented; they’re just a smaller, squatter take on the Pixel Watch tile system, and it’s one of the best things about the Fitbit Edge interface. It’s also really snappy, which is something that isn’t the case with cheaper fitness trackers such as this. I’m constantly checking the weather or using the Google Health tile, but I have loved the quick access complication on the default watch face.

I tried a few of the other designs over the past 30 days; a lot of them are great. The default has become my favorite. It’s information-dense without being too overloaded. Tapping the complications takes you to the exact data point. I genuinely love how fuss-free an experience it is, save for a few minor complaints.

We could criticize the accuracy of the data or the lack of tracking for certain types of workouts, but I think that misses the point of the Fitbit Edge. It’s a simple tracker with a screen, and the fact that you get even basic ECG on a device of this size is impressive.

I truly have worn the Edge daily for a full month, and while the bands are comfortable, I have found that they cause me to get a rash on the underside of my left wrist just under the palm. It’s actively stopping me from wearing it all the time now. I hope that the new connector doesn’t slow down third-party development for bands, because I’m desperate for a fabric band to alleviate this issue.

It has been revealed that this is exacerbated when the rubber band gets wet or sweaty. If you have sensitive skin, you might have the same problem as I have. Using some moisturizer has helped, but it is something I wasn’t prepared to suffer with before the Fitbit Edge turned up. I get that this is likely a “me” problem, but I wanted to note it.

Sources indicate that when the screen gets wet or moist, it can bug out quite a lot. Taps don’t register properly, and a few water droplets can activate all the menus and submenus. Luckily, it won’t force your phone to place a call or anything like that, but the water protection mode is a must. I have kept it on extensively.

Swimmers will probably get super frustrated; heck, I was on a rainy day as the screen kept bugging out. Overall, though, I have enjoyed the fitness tracking. Unlike on the Fitbit Air, it is nice to have a screen to start a workout rather than head over to my phone. That remarked, the experience is the same as on your phone, but scaled down to fit the watch face.

According to recent reports, I dislike that you don’t get a phone notification to show the current workout progress by default, like the Fitbit Air. I had become accustomed to that. Luckily, you can enable it in the Google Health settings. I like having this as I forget to stop workouts so often without a prompt to hit “stop.”.

It has been revealed that with audio playback, you’re also getting the partial benefits of watch-phone controls, but it’s a two-step process unlike on Pixel Watch. You either have to go to the “Media” app or have the tile active and navigate to it to access play/pause and all your other streaming app controls. I tend not to bother using these as it’s finicky.

This had me thinking about NFC. I think a lot of people would have liked NFC for Google Wallet on the Fitbit Edge, but I think having to enter a PIN on such a small screen would really have been a nightmare. I’ve made wireless payments with my watch less than five times, as it’s just easier to use my phone rather than contort my wrist to a wireless payment terminal. I figure this was something that was thought about and makes a lot of sense given the constraints.

Recent findings suggest that one of my other complaints is that the DND and Bedtime modes from my account haven’t synced or at least don’t appear to sync. Unless I’m mistaken, you need to activate these settings manually every time, which has been super annoying when in bed, as a flick of your wrist can blind you in a dark room. I figure this is something that can be fixed with an update, so here’s hoping.

I’ve been super impressed with the battery life. A week is easily attainable for me with up to three gym visits per week, so I’ve charged 5 times in a month. That, to me, is excellent. I picked up a cheap charging dock, as the Edge uses the same charger for the Fitbit Air, so I figured why not.

It’s not the best-looking dock, but I quite like how it airs off my Edge so it’s not as stinky after gym sessions – as I wipe with an alcohol pad and clean as regularly as possible.

It has been revealed that the experience is fine; it’s almost a third of the price of the Pixel Watch and lacks a few features due to the various compromises – compromises I can deal with, as smartwatches have become information overload for me over time, and I like that the app selection is ultra-refined. At no point does the Fitbit Edge give you information overload.

Recent findings suggest that coming from a Charge 6 or an older Fitbit, this is an amazing replacement. It’s the upcoming “default” fitness tracker for people who want all the hallmarks of what makes a great Fitbit.

Recent findings suggest that there is just enough. Nothing more, nothing less. To me, this feels like the perfect middle ground for a lot of people. You want something simple, touchscreen-enabled, and that doesn’t get in the way. As impressed as I have been with the Edge, though, I’ve loved a fuss-free tech accessory so much recently that I’ll probably go back to the Fitbit Air.
